title: JSON columns, indexes, and functions
summary: Store, index, query, and shape semi-structured JSON in SQL Server — and see exactly how PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Oracle differ.

items: Store JSON in SQL Server using the native json data type and the nvarchar pattern.
Query and shape JSON with OPENJSON, JSON_VALUE, JSON_QUERY, JSON_OBJECT, and JSON_ARRAY.
Translate JSON designs across SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Oracle.

blocks.body: Modern applications mix relational and semi-structured data. DP-800 expects you to store JSON, validate it, extract and project values, and index it for performance. SQL Server 2025 adds a native `json` data type alongside the long-standing `nvarchar(max)` approach.

terms.definition: SQL Server 2025's native binary JSON type with validation and efficient access.
Table-valued function that shreds a JSON document into rows and columns.
Extracts a scalar value from JSON using a path expression.
A `$.a.b[0]` expression that navigates into a JSON document.

blocks.heading: Storing JSON
blocks.body: SQL Server 2025 introduces the native **`json`** data type, which stores an optimized binary form, validates on insert, and speeds up read/modify operations. Before it, JSON was stored in `nvarchar(max)` with an optional `ISJSON()` check constraint. Both are still valid; the exam expects you to know the native type is preferred on SQL Server 2025.

blocks.heading: Reading JSON
blocks.body:
- **`JSON_VALUE(expr, path)`** returns a scalar (string/number).
- **`JSON_QUERY(expr, path)`** returns an object or array fragment.
- **`OPENJSON(expr [, path]) WITH (...)`** shreds JSON into a rowset with a typed schema.
- **`ISJSON(expr)`** validates.

blocks.heading: Constructing JSON
blocks.body: SQL Server supports **`JSON_OBJECT`**, **`JSON_ARRAY`**, and **`JSON_ARRAYAGG`** constructors, plus **`FOR JSON PATH`/`AUTO`** to serialize query results. **`JSON_MODIFY`** updates values in place, and **`JSON_CONTAINS`** tests membership.

blocks.caption: How OPENJSON shreds a document into a typed rowset that you can join like any table.
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    doc["JSON document {orders:[...] }"] --> openjson["OPENJSON(@json, '$.orders')"]
    openjson --> withclause["WITH (id INT, total DECIMAL)"]
    withclause --> rows["Relational rowset"]
    rows --> joins["JOIN / WHERE / aggregate"]

blocks.heading: Native json column + query
blocks.body:
```sql
-- SQL Server 2025 native json type
CREATE TABLE dbo.Product (
    ProductId INT PRIMARY KEY,
    Attributes json NOT NULL
);

INSERT dbo.Product VALUES
(1, '{"color":"red","tags":["sale","new"],"dims":{"w":10,"h":4}}');

-- Scalar extract
SELECT ProductId,
       JSON_VALUE(Attributes, '$.color')   AS color,
       JSON_QUERY(Attributes, '$.tags')    AS tags
FROM dbo.Product;

-- Shred an array into rows
SELECT p.ProductId, t.[value] AS tag
FROM dbo.Product p
CROSS APPLY OPENJSON(p.Attributes, '$.tags') t;
```

blocks.heading: Indexing JSON predicates
PostgreSQL: jsonb + GIN
MySQL: JSON type + generated columns
Oracle: JSON type + JSON_TABLE

comparison.title: JSON support
comparison.description: All four engines store and query JSON, but indexing strategy and function names differ significantly.

migration.equivalent: Storing documents and extracting scalar values is conceptually identical across all four engines.
migration.different: Index strategy differs the most: PostgreSQL jsonb indexes the whole document with GIN, while SQL Server and MySQL require promoting paths to (computed/generated) columns.
migration.directMigration: Partial. Data migrates cleanly; queries and index DDL must be rewritten per engine.
migration.syntaxChanges: Replace JSON_VALUE/OPENJSON with the target engine's operators (->>, JSON_TABLE, jsonb_array_elements).
migration.limitations: SQL Server's native json type is 2025-only; older targets need nvarchar(max) + ISJSON.
migration.whenToUse: Use jsonb (PostgreSQL) when you need flexible ad-hoc indexing of documents; use the native json types elsewhere when documents are read via known paths.

blocks.heading: Product catalog with variable attributes
blocks.body: A catalog has thousands of product types with different attributes. Store the stable columns relationally (id, price, name) and put variable attributes in a `json` column. Promote the two or three attributes you filter on (color, brand) to computed/generated columns and index those. This keeps writes flexible while queries stay fast — the pattern the exam rewards.

items.mistake: Expecting a JSON path predicate to use an index automatically.
items.fix: On SQL Server and MySQL, promote the path to a computed/generated column and index it; only PostgreSQL jsonb indexes the document directly.

items.mistake: Using JSON_VALUE to return an object or array.
items.fix: JSON_VALUE returns scalars only; use JSON_QUERY for object/array fragments.
Keep columns you join/filter/aggregate on relational; use JSON for genuinely variable data.

blocks.body: Validate input with `ISJSON()` (or an `IS JSON` check) to avoid storing malformed documents. Large JSON blobs bloat memory grants — project only the paths you need. Treat JSON extracted into dynamic SQL as untrusted input to avoid injection.

tips: OPENJSON with an explicit WITH clause returns strongly-typed columns — the go-to for shredding.
JSON_VALUE = scalar; JSON_QUERY = object/array. This distinction shows up often.
Remember the native json data type is a SQL Server 2025 addition.

blocks.body: SQL Server stores JSON in the native json type (2025) or nvarchar(max), reads it with JSON_VALUE/JSON_QUERY/OPENJSON, and indexes it via computed columns. PostgreSQL's jsonb + GIN is the most flexible for ad-hoc indexing; MySQL and Oracle sit in between. Keep hot, structured data relational and reserve JSON for truly variable attributes.
